Looping in product/reliability notes for the Nimbus eval. High level answers (I can expand into the matrix attached):

- Uptime guarantees: Redwood offers a platform SLO of 99.95% for hosted API endpoints (monthly). For Dedicated customers we provide SLA-backed uptime with crediting; for this eval we should show historical 6-month uptime for tenant-like workloads (I can export).

- Rate limiting / throttling: per-tenant token buckets per route + circuit-breaker tiers. We do graceful 429 throttling with informative headers (X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-Quota-Reset) and an automatic short-circuit fallback to a smaller model variant when per-route CPU/KV cache pressure is detected. That fallback avoids complete hard failures and significantly reduces tail error budgets compared to opaque hyperscaler throttles.

- Error budget definition: Aligns with what Alex noted; we measure p99 success rate and track rolling 30d error budget burn. Alerts trigger at 10% burn and paging at 50% burn with automated mitigation policies (traffic diversion, autoscale).

- Failover behavior: Redwood supports zone-aware routing and warm-standby model variants across regions. On simulated zone outage we fail traffic to healthy pools within ~15-30s depending on active KV cache warming; we record the controlled degradation (increase in latency) rather than blind drops. See attached slo-comparison-matrix.xlsx for comparison vs typical hyperscaler-managed endpoints (cold-start amplifications, blunt throttling).

Attachments: slo-comparison-matrix.xlsx, redwood-failover-runbook.pdf

Action items I can cover: export 6-month uptime for a tenant-sized workload, provision sandbox endpoints, and enumerate exact header semantics for our throttling responses. Marissa — if you can confirm the sandbox accounts and the target soak window with Nimbus, I'll queue infra to freeze the hosts during the soak window per their ask.

—Ben
